title: Lumley v. Wagner
lead: A singer’s engagement combined a promise to perform at one London theatre with an express promise not to perform elsewhere. The Chancellor enforced the latter while acknowledging that equity could not command the performances themselves.

actors.name: Joseph Bacher
actors.role: Agent involved in arranging the engagement

proceedings: Vice-Chancellor Parker granted an injunction on May 9, 1852.
Lord Chancellor St. Leonards heard the appeal motion on May 22 and 26.
Motion to discharge the injunction refused with costs.
limits: Historical 1852 injunction ruling, not an order to sing, damages award, or adjudication of a later tort action. Earlier Hills judgment reproduced in a note and later editorial commentary are not separate Lumley opinions.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An engagement gains an exclusivity term
paragraphs: Benjamin Lumley leased Her Majesty’s Theatre in London. Through Joseph Bacher, he arranged a French-language agreement at Berlin on November 9, 1851, for Johanna Wagner to sing there for three months beginning April 1, 1852, generally twice each week. Six operatic parts were identified and reserved to her, with the first three performances ordered. Pay was £400 monthly, in weekly £100 payments, with £50 for an additional performance. Lumley would advance £300 at Berlin on March 15, recovered through monthly deductions. The agreement separately addressed illness, delayed arrival, and transfer to a successor.

According to Lumley’s later bill, the initial writing omitted his requested exclusivity. When Bacher met him in Paris that November, Lumley objected and Bacher added an article as the Wagners’ authorized agent. Johanna promised not to sing at another theatre, public or private concert, or reunion without Lumley’s written permission.

sections.title: A competing engagement produces an injunction
paragraphs: Lumley alleged that Johanna and her father Albert subsequently arranged higher-paid performances for Frederick Gye, the lessee of Covent Garden Theatre, and intended to abandon his engagement. He alleged that Gye knew of the prior contract. The Wagners repudiated on the ground that Lumley had not fulfilled its financial requirements; their answer also challenged Bacher’s authority to add the restriction.

Lumley filed his bill on April 22, 1852, asking to restrain Johanna’s competing performances, Albert’s sanctioning them, and Gye’s accepting her services without permission. Vice-Chancellor Sir James Parker granted an injunction on May 9. The defendants sought its discharge before Lord Chancellor St. Leonards. Although the motion reached him on the representation that argument would concern equity’s jurisdiction, he also addressed the factual objections.

sections.title: Can equity enforce the promised abstention?
paragraphs: The defendants argued that equity could not specifically enforce personal services and therefore could not restrain breach of the associated negative promise. They considered damages sufficient and maintained that the injunction would indirectly compel an agreement the court could not execute as a whole. They relied on Kemble v. Kean and Kimberley v. Jennings and sought to distinguish contrary cases as partnerships or substantially completed agreements. Lumley answered that he sought enforcement of the negative undertaking itself and also pointed to preparations and expenditure for the operas.

St. Leonards rejected the proposed categorical restriction. Decisions concerning bell ringing, leased property, and professional apprentices showed that injunction jurisdiction did not depend on power to compel every affirmative obligation. A legal remedy did not itself exclude equity. Practical difficulty in administering a restraint could justify refusing relief, but that concerned exercising jurisdiction, not its existence.

Here the affirmative and negative promises operated together: competing performances would defeat the engagement’s purpose. The Chancellor acknowledged that restraint might induce Wagner to perform, but distinguished that consequence from an order commanding her to sing. Although he said competition would violate the engagement’s spirit even without an express restriction, he expressly stated that an affirmative promise alone would not have supported this injunction. He enforced the actual negative article.

sections.title: Precedent and the factual objections
paragraphs: The Chancellor considered Kemble wrongly decided and understood Rolfe v. Rolfe to undermine the earlier contrary decisions. Clarke v. Price lacked a negative promise and could not support compelled reporting services. He retained the concern illustrated by Hills v. Croll: restraining a purchaser to one supplier could ruin the purchaser if equity could not compel that supplier’s continuing performance. The Hills judgment reproduced in a note was an earlier decision, not another opinion in Wagner’s case.

Turning to the evidence, St. Leonards found the Wagners had acquiesced in the restriction’s remaining, whatever Bacher’s initial authority. The engagement had first been postponed for their convenience. Lumley had to tender the advance before obtaining equitable relief, and the £300 had been paid to the parties’ common agent for transmission.

A final evidentiary ruling supported that conclusion. Bacher swore that his letter acknowledged receipt and offered payment according to Johanna’s instructions. She admitted receiving a letter of that date but disputed its contents. With the original absent without explanation and no retained copy, the Chancellor accepted Bacher’s affidavit: when swearing it, Bacher could not have known the letter would be withheld and risked immediate contradiction. On jurisdiction and the merits presented, the Chancellor refused the motion with costs. The existing restraint remained; Wagner was not ordered to sing and no damages were awarded.
